title: Preparing an executive presentation deck on Mac: a 2026 routine for product managers
metaTitle: Preparing an executive presentation deck on Mac for PMs
description: Preparing an executive presentation deck eats more PM time than it should. Get a weekly routine, slide fixes for PowerPoint and Keynote, and where Lazur helps.
intro: To prepare an executive presentation deck on Mac, write the decision you need from the room before you open PowerPoint or Keynote. Then build the slides backward from that one ask, and add only the evidence that supports it. This page covers what the work costs, why decks run late, fixes you can use today, and where Lazur helps.
tldr: Write the decision and a one-page answer before you open any slide software.
Decks run late for reasons you can name: an unclear ask, numbers that keep moving, and too much on each slide.
Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index shows PowerPoint edits spike 122% in the 10 minutes before a meeting.
Designer and Copilot help with layouts, but they have limits and plan requirements. Check them first.
Lazur can point, explain, guide and draft text. It does not edit your deck or click for you.

blocks.text: What an executive deck has to do

An executive deck has one job. It gets a decision, a sign-off, or a budget from people who have little time. Everything else on the slides supports that job. Most decks fail because they try to show everything you learned, so they read like a report with a title page.

That is why preparing an executive presentation deck takes longer than the slides suggest. You are not only making slides. You are deciding what the room should conclude, then proving it in a few minutes. Some leaders skim the title and first slide before a meeting. Some get the deck as a pre-read and never hear you talk. Build the first page to stand alone.
What the prep time really costs

Start with time, because it is the cost you feel first. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index found that workers get interrupted about every two minutes. That works out to 275 interruptions a day. A deck needs one long, quiet stretch. If your calendar has no such gap, deck work spills into evenings and weekends.

Then there is rework. A deck that goes through several rounds of 'can you change this slide' costs more than one that is right early. Each comment reopens a slide, and each reopened slide pulls in the charts behind it. That time rarely shows up in a planning doc.

Put a rough price on your hours. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a May 2025 median hourly wage of $79.70 for advertising, promotions, and marketing managers. That is not a PM job title, so use it as a loose anchor for senior, non-engineering time. TextDeck, a vendor that sells an AI presentation tool, estimates executives spend 3 to 5 hours a week on presentation work without AI. Its sources are unnamed. At $79.70 an hour, that range is roughly $240 to $400 a week. Treat the result as a conversation starter, not a finance number.

blocks.text: Look at the symptom first, then trace it back. Underneath most of these, the slides came before the decision. You open PowerPoint because you feel you should be doing something. The deck then grows around the material you already have. The fix sits upstream of the slides.
Write the one-page answer first

items: Write the decision in one sentence that starts with a verb: approve, fund, pick, or stop.
Write three reasons in plain sentences. Each reason should be a claim, not a topic.
List the evidence each claim needs. Mark anything you cannot source as a gap, not a fact.
Write the risk and the fallback in plain words. Say what happens if the bet fails.
Only then open PowerPoint or Keynote and make one slide per claim.

blocks.text: The method that helps most here is the one-page answer. It sits close to what Barbara Minto calls the Pyramid Principle, which leads with the answer and supports it with grouped reasons. I did not find a controlled study that tests the Pyramid Principle. Treat it as a method to test on your own reviews, not as proven science.
Build slides an executive can read fast

Research on slides gives you a few firm rules. Kosslyn and colleagues analyzed 140 PowerPoint slideshows against 137 rules. Under strict scoring, each slideshow broke, on average, 6.23 of nine principle classes. None was flawless. The most common breaks involved bullets that build one at a time, which 96% of slideshows violated, and lists with more than four bullets, which 91% had.

Mayer and Fiorella reviewed multimedia learning research in the Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning. The coherence principle says to leave out extra material. It was supported in 23 of 23 experimental tests. The redundancy principle says not to put on-screen text that repeats your narration. It was supported in 16 of 16 tests. Those tests come from learning research, not from executive reviews. The advice still fits a room that has to decide fast.
Use PowerPoint Designer and Copilot on Mac

PowerPoint for Mac includes Designer, which suggests slide layouts. Microsoft says Designer is only for Microsoft 365 subscribers, and some organizations turn it off. To stop automatic suggestions, open Preferences > General > Authoring and Proofing Tools > PowerPoint Designer. Clear Automatically show me design ideas. Microsoft lists Version 15.26.0.160910 or later on the Monthly Channel as the Mac minimum.

blocks.title: Designer skips some slides
blocks.text: Designer cannot suggest layouts for a slide that has a drawn shape or a text box. The slide must use the Title or Title + Content layout. Designer also stops working when more than one person co-edits the slide. Check those limits before you blame the feature.

Microsoft says Copilot in PowerPoint is available on Windows, Mac and the web, under Microsoft 365. Brand Kit needs a separate Microsoft Copilot license. Use Copilot to tighten a draft or adjust tone. Do not use it to choose your claim. That decision still belongs to you, and the reviewer will ask about it.
Keynote on Mac, if your team uses it

Keynote 15.4 requires macOS 26 or later, according to Apple's Get started guide. Check your version under Apple menu > About This Mac. The guide covers themes with layouts, Content Hub objects, animations, export to PDF, PowerPoint and movie, and rehearsal. It does not list AI features or presenter note generation. Plan to write your own speaker notes, and export to PowerPoint if your leader needs an Office file.
Protect confidential numbers and follow employer rules

Exec decks often carry revenue, roadmap dates, and customer names. Before you paste any of that into an AI tool, read your employer's policy. Some companies approve specific tools. Others block AI tools on work data. Your employer's rule comes before any advice on this page, including this one.

Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer your question, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those facts help you judge the tool. They do not replace your company's rules.

blocks.text: Notice what changed. The analysis did not get better. The order did. The leader reads the ask in the first few seconds and can stop there if they agree. The appendix still holds the history, so nobody loses the detail.
Mistakes that send a deck back

items: Putting full analysis on the main slides instead of in the appendix.
Writing a topic title, like Pricing review, instead of a claim.
Sending the deck as a pre-read with no note that says what you need.
Changing a number the morning of the review without telling the data owner.
Presenting every slide when the first three already got the decision.
Letting Designer rearrange a slide that holds a carefully drawn diagram.

blocks.text: Rehearse the questions, not only the slides

Most exec reviews turn on two or three questions. Write them down before the meeting. For each question, write a short answer and name the slide that backs it. Keep the answers in your speaker notes or the appendix, so you can find them under pressure.

Dictation helps with this step. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor in any app. Dictate each answer into a note, then cut it down by hand. You can also ask Lazur to draft a first pass from the question list you paste in. Rewrite the draft in your own words, and check every number against its source.
Where to start this week

Pick one upcoming deck and run it through the one-page answer method before you open slide software. Watch where the time goes. If it goes into rework, fix the ask. If it goes into layout, try Designer within its limits. If it goes into chasing numbers, that is a data problem, and no slide tool fixes it.

faq.question: How long does preparing an executive presentation deck take?
faq.answer: No study I found measures how many hours PMs spend on this. A vendor estimate puts executives at 3 to 5 hours a week on presentation work without AI, from unnamed sources. Track one deck from start to finish to get your own number. Log the rework rounds too.

faq.question: How many slides should an executive deck have?
faq.answer: There is no sourced rule for the right count. Aim for the fewest slides that carry one decision. Move methods, full tables, and history to an appendix. A short main section is easier to defend in the room than a long one.

faq.question: Is PowerPoint Designer worth using on Mac?
faq.answer: It can help on simple slides that use the Title or Title + Content layout. Designer needs a Microsoft 365 subscription, and some organizations turn it off. It cannot suggest layouts for slides with drawn shapes or text boxes. Test it on one slide first.

faq.question: Can Lazur build my slides?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points, explains, guides, dictates and drafts text. It does not click buttons or edit your deck. Ask it where a setting is, or ask it to walk you through a change one click at a time.

faq.question: Is it safe to put deck numbers into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Check your employer's policy first. Some companies approve specific tools and block others. Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Does Keynote have AI slide features on Mac?
faq.answer: Apple's Keynote 15.4 guide, which requires macOS 26 or later, does not list AI features or presenter note generation. Apple may change features over time, so check the current guide before you plan around one.

faq.question: What is the Pyramid Principle?
faq.answer: It is a structure from Barbara Minto that leads with the answer, then supports it with grouped reasons. I did not find a controlled study that tests it. Use it as a method, then judge it on your own reviews.

costs.title: Calendar time that never shows up
costs.text: Deck work needs long, uninterrupted blocks. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index reports workers are interrupted about every two minutes, which is 275 interruptions a day. Each switch costs you the thread of the argument, so the deck takes longer than the hours you logged.

costs.title: Rounds of rework
costs.text: A deck that goes through several rounds of edits costs more than one that is right early. Each reviewer asks for one change, and each change reopens a slide. You rarely log that time, so it stays out of your planning.

costs.title: Salary time at a rough rate
costs.text: BLS lists a May 2025 median of $79.70 an hour for marketing managers. That is a proxy, not a PM rate. TextDeck estimates executives spend 3 to 5 hours a week on presentations without AI, from unnamed sources. Together those inputs point to roughly $240 to $400 a week in salary time.

costs.title: Decisions that arrive late
costs.text: A deck that hides the ask can push a decision into the next review cycle. That cost shows up in the roadmap, not on your timesheet. Name that cost when you ask for a longer review slot, so the delay has a price attached.

causes.title: The slides come before the decision
causes.text: Opening PowerPoint feels like progress. The deck then grows around the material you have, not the choice you need. Without one decision in the title, every reviewer reads the deck differently and asks for a different slide.

causes.title: Data arrives late and keeps changing
causes.text: Numbers move while you build. You rebuild charts, the story shifts, and the slides you polished no longer fit. If nobody freezes the data, the deck never closes, and the final week turns into a scramble.

causes.title: Clutter the audience has to filter
causes.text: Kosslyn and colleagues found typical slides broke basic cognitive principles. Discriminability and limited capacity were violated in 100% of the slideshows they analyzed. Dense slides make the room work to find your point, and that point is what you need them to remember.

causes.title: Interruptions and meeting-day edits
causes.text: Microsoft reports PowerPoint edits spike 122% in the 10 minutes before a meeting. That pattern points to last-minute fixes. Last-minute fixes tend to add slides, not remove them, so the deck grows right before it is judged.

causes.title: No named reviewer or sign-off path
causes.text: When nobody owns the decision, every comment becomes a new request. The deck stays open, and each reviewer asks for one more slide. A named reviewer and a named decision are what end that loop.

fixes.title: Write the ask as a verb sentence
fixes.text: Start the decision with a verb: approve, fund, pick or stop. Put that sentence on the title slide and in the message that sends the deck. A reviewer who reads one line should know what you want. If you cannot write it in one sentence, you are not ready to build slides.

fixes.title: Freeze the data before review week
fixes.text: Pick the day your numbers stop changing. Write that cut date on the first slide, next to the source. Any later change goes to the data owner as a note, with the old and new figure side by side. Silent swaps cost trust fast.

fixes.title: Book one quiet block for deck work
fixes.text: Put a long block on your calendar and treat it like a meeting. On Mac, turn on a Focus in System Settings > Focus so Slack and mail stay quiet during that block. Use the time for the one-page answer and the first draft, not for email.

fixes.title: Test the deck with titles only
fixes.text: Read only the slide titles, in order. If the titles tell a clear story that ends in the ask, the deck works. If they read like a table of contents, rewrite the titles before you touch the visuals. This test takes minutes and catches most structure problems.

fixes.title: Move detail to an appendix
fixes.text: Keep the main section to the decision, the reasons, the evidence for each reason, and the risk. Put methods, full tables and history after a divider slide labeled Appendix. You can still show it when a reviewer asks, without making everyone sit through it.

fixes.title: Name one first-page reviewer
fixes.text: Choose one person to read only the first page before the deck goes wide. Ask them what they would decide from that page alone. Their answer tells you whether the ask lands, and it comes faster than another full review.

fixes.title: Check Mac and plan limits before you rely on a feature
fixes.text: Designer needs a Microsoft 365 subscription and a current PowerPoint build. Keynote 15.4 needs macOS 26. Open Apple menu > About This Mac to check your version. Check your organization's settings too, since some turn features off.

fixes.title: Rehearse the three hardest questions
fixes.text: Write the three questions most likely to stall the decision. Answer each in two sentences, out loud. Then name the slide that holds the proof. If you cannot find that slide in a few seconds, move it earlier in the deck.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Write the ask
plan.text: Write the decision in one sentence before you open any deck software. Draft three reasons in plain text. Mark every claim you cannot source as a gap to close before Wednesday.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Gather and freeze the evidence
plan.text: Pull the numbers into Google Sheets or your data tool. Label each chart with the claim it proves. Freeze the data cut and write the date on the first slide.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Build from the claims
plan.text: Make one slide per claim in your deck tool. Use Designer only on slides with the Title or Title + Content layout. Move detail to the appendix as you go.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Get one early read
plan.text: Send the one-page answer, not the full deck, to one reviewer. Ask what they would decide from the first page alone. Change the ask if their answer surprises you.

plan.label: Day before
plan.title: Rehearse the hard questions
plan.text: Say the three hardest questions out loud. Dictate short answers with fn into a note, then cut them down to plain sentences. Check the proof slide for each answer.

plan.label: Meeting day
plan.title: Check the first page
plan.text: Open the deck to the first slide. Confirm the ask on screen matches the one you sent. If you blank, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur about anything on screen.
